Introduction
Authors and management experts have defined research in various ways. 
Typically, research is said to commence with a question or a problem. It is described 
as the creation of new concepts, methodologies, and understandings through the 
development of new knowledge or the innovative application of existing knowledge. 
This process often involves synthesizing and analysing previous studies to produce 
new and groundbreaking results.
1.1 Research
Through research, we can identify solutions to problems by employing systematic 
and scientific methods. This may involve experimentation or innovation, with “risk” 
highlighting the inherent dangers of discovery. 
1.1.1 Definition and Objectives of Research
What is research?
Investigation might lead to analysis, and tests could be conducted to verify 
hypotheses. This work is distinct and unprecedented, offering new insights as a 
result. It could introduce a novel method or new data source, leading to significant 
breakthroughs or incremental improvements in current practices. Research is essential 
for progress, as it is fundamentally tied to “research and development.”
Slesinger & Stephenson, Encyclopaedia of Social Sciences:
“the manipulation of things, concepts or symbols for the purpose of generalizing to 
extend, correct or verify knowledge, whether that knowledge aids in the construction of 
theory or in the practice of an art”.
●
●
Redman & Mory: “Systematized effort to gain new knowledge”. It is an academic 
activity and should be used in a technical sense.
●
●
Clifford Woody: Research comprises “defining and redefining problems, 
formulating hypotheses or suggested solutions; collecting, organizing and 
evaluating data; making deductions and reaching conclusions; and finally, carefully 
testing the conclusions to determine whether they fit the formulated hypotheses”.
Research Objectives
General Objectives
General objectives, also known as secondary objectives, provide a detailed view

of a study’s goal. In other words, by the end of your studies, you will have a general 
idea of what you want to accomplish. For instance, your overarching objective can 
be to look at the organisation’s usage of renewable energy sources and sustainable 
practices in order to determine how much the organisation contributes to environmental 
sustainability.
Specific Objectives
Specific objectives outline the primary aim of a study. Typically, general objectives 
provide the basis for establishing specific goals. Essentially, specific objectives are 
general objectives that have been divided into smaller, logically interconnected goals. 
They assist you in defining the who, what, why, when, and how of your project. It’s 
much easier to develop and carry out a research plan once you’ve identified the main 
goal.
Take, for example, a study of an organisation’s contribution to environmental 
sustainability. The specific goals will be as follows:
●
●
Determine how the organisation has changed its practises and adopted new 
solutions throughout its history.
●
●
To determine the impact of new practices, technology, and strategies on overall 
effectiveness.
1.1.2: Characteristics of Research
● 
The research should concentrate on the most pressing issues.
● 
The investigation should be methodical. It emphasises the importance of following a 
structured procedure when conducting research.
● 
The research should follow a logical pattern. The scientific researcher cannot make 
much progress in any investigation without manipulating ideas logically.
● 
The study should be condensed. This means that a researcher’s findings should 
be made available to other researchers so that they don’t have to repeat the same 
research.
● 
The findings should be repeatable. This states that results from earlier studies have 
to be verifiable in new locations, environments, with fresh people, or at a different 
time.
● 
The research ought to be successful. The fact that a single research topic may spark 
the creation of several others is one of its most significant features.
● 
Action-oriented research is required. In other words, it should aim to find a solution 
that will allow its findings to be implemented.
● 
The research should take an integrated multidisciplinary approach, which means it 
will require research approaches from multiple disciplines.
● 
At all stages of the study, all parties involved (from policymakers to community 
members) should be invited to participate.
● 
The research has to have an easy-to-understand design and be conducted within a 
specific timeframe.
● 
As little money as feasible should be spent on the research.
● 
Formats that are most helpful to administrators, decision-makers, company managers, 
or community members should be used to deliver the study findings.

1.1.3 Differences b/w Research Methods and Research Methodology
Although the names sound similar, both Research methods and Research 
methodology are different, as explained below:
Research Methods
The various procedures, schemes, steps, and algorithms used in research are 
known as research methods. The term “research methods” refers to all of the methods 
used by a researcher during a research study. They’re primarily planned, scientific, and 
value-agnostic. Observations, theoretical procedures, experimental studies, numerical 
schemes, statistical approaches, and so on are all examples of these. We can use 
research methods to collect samples, data, and come up with a solution to a problem. 
Business and scientific research methods, in particular, demand explanations based on 
collected facts, measurements, and observations, rather than solely on reasoning. They 
only accept explanations that can be verified through experiments.
Research Methodology
A systematic approach to solving a problem is known as research methodology. It 
is a science that studies how research should be conducted. Research methodology 
is essentially the procedures by which researchers go about their work of describing, 
explaining, and predicting phenomena. It can also be defined as the study of methods 
for gaining knowledge. Its goal is to provide a research work plan.
1.2 Research Process
In the early decades human inquiry was primarily based on the examination of 
one’s own conscious thoughts and feelings that means the observation of any one and 
understanding through logical discussion to seek the truth. This process served as a 
well-established conceptual framework for comprehending the world and was accepted 
for a century. An essential component of the investigation process was the knowledge 
seeker. With time, this part was changed. The Scientific method introduced several 
major components in research procedures like Objectivity. 
1.2.1 Research Criteria and Research Process
Research Criteria:
● 
The goal of the study should be made very clear, and common principles should be 
applied.
● 
There should be enough description of the research process. in such a way as 
to preserve the integrity of the work previously completed while enabling another 
researcher to carry out the research for future development.
● 
To get unbiased outcomes, the procedural design of the research should be carefully 
prepared.
● 
Any shortcomings in the technique design should be fully disclosed by the researcher, 
along with an assessment of how they could affect the results.
● 
The analytic techniques employed should be suitable, and the data should be 
sufficiently analysed to demonstrate its relevance. Verification of the data’s legitimacy 
and dependability is necessary.

Only conclusions that are bolstered by the study findings and for which the facts

If the researcher is experienced, has a good research reputation, and is a person of

Research Process:
Planning must be done methodically at every step of the marketing research 
process. The methods at each step are systematic, meticulously recorded, and, to the 
greatest degree possible, time-scheduled. In order to examine theories or preconceived 
beliefs, marketing research employs the scientific method, which involves gathering and 
analysing data.
For reliable information that accurately reflects the scenario, marketing research 
should be carried out impartially. The study should be impartial and devoid of 
the personal or political prejudices of the researcher or management, even if the 
researcher’s research philosophy will always have an impact on the findings.
For instance, we could discover that the project’s scope is insufficient, that our 
topic is too wide and has to be limited, that there aren’t enough information resources 
accessible, or that the material we gather contradicts our thesis.
There are nine main steps of the research process that are followed at the time of 
designing a research project. They are as follows.
Step 1: Problem Definition
Step 2: Development of an Approach to the Problem
Step 3: Research Design Formulation
Step 4: Field Work or Data Collection
Step 5: Data Preparation and Analysis
Step 6: Report Preparation and Presentation
1.2.2: Approaches of Research: Deductive, Inductive, Quantitative 
and Qualitative
Deductive: Deductive approach starts with developing a hypothesis based on 
existing theory, and then prepares a research strategy for testing the hypothesis. To 
reason deductively is to go from the specific to the general. In many circumstances, 
a theory or case study that suggests a causal relationship or correlation may be 
accurate. The term “deductive approach” refers to a method of formulating hypotheses 
or drawing conclusions from theoretical ideas. The deductive method is concerned with 
drawing conclusions from statements or premises. By “testing against observations,” 
deductive reasoning begins with a pattern, whereas induction methodology “begins with 
observations and seeks to find a pattern within them.”
Benefits of Deductive:
● 
Probability to clarify the relationships between variables and concepts.
● 
Probability to measure concepts in a quantitative manner.
● 
Probability to generalize research findings to a certain extent.

This approach mainly follows the given stages, like
1.

Inductive: Inductive approach or inductive reasoning, starts with observations and 
theories are proposed which are related to the conclusion of the investigation due to 
the findings. It entails looking for patterns in observations and creating theories—or 
explanations—for those patterns by formulating a number of conjectures. In inductive 
studies, at the beginning of the research neither theories nor hypotheses would apply 
and the researcher is free to alter the direction for the study after the research process 
had commenced.
Using an inductive method to formulate research questions and objectives 
does not entail ignoring theories. By finding patterns and linkages in the data set, 
this method aids in the generation of interpretations from which a theory may be 
developed. This approach is mainly based on learning from experience. Previous 
patterns, resemblances and regularities are observed in order to reach conclusions or 
to generate theory.
 
Abductive Reasoning or Abductive Approach
Abductive reasoning is set to address weaknesses associated with deductive and 
inductive approaches. Specifically for deductive reasoning ‘ how to select theory to be 
tested via formulating hypotheses’ and for Inductive reasoning “no amount of empirical 
data will necessarily enable theory-building”. It acts as a third alternative, overcoming 
these weaknesses via adopting a pragmatist perspective.

It is clear that abductive reasoning is similar to deductive and inductive approaches 
in a way that it is applied to make logical inferences and construct theories.
Abductive approaches begin with “surprising facts’’ or “puzzles,” and the goal of 
the research process is to figure out how to explain them. A researcher may come into 
“surprising facts’ ‘ or “puzzles’ ‘ when they come across an empirical phenomenon that 
the current theories are unable to explain. In that approach, researchers search for the 
‘best explanation among many alternatives to choose. Researchers can combine both, 
numerical and cognitive reasoning for explaining ‘surprising facts’ or ‘puzzles’.
Qualitative research: It is a non-statistical process of inquiry. It helps with in-depth 
understanding of problems or issues in their natural settings. It is highly based on the 
researchers’ background and the sample-probing questions they employed. Usually, 
there are restrictions on the sample size in between a minimum of 6 and a maximum of 
10 people. Open-ended questions are asked( to gather as much information as possible 
from the sample )in a manner that encourages answers that lead to another question or 
a group of questions. The below methods are used for qualitative research:
1. One-to-one interview
2.	 Focus groups
3.	 Ethnographic research
4.	 Content/Text analysis
5.	 Case study research
Quantitative research: A systematic approach to gathering data and interpreting 
it to make inferences is known as quantitative research. This approach gathers 
and analyses data using a statistical and computational procedure. The main focus 
of quantitative data is numbers. A greater population is involved because more 
individuals will contribute more data which helps to obtain more accurate results. This 
research uses close-ended questions because the researchers are typically looking 
to gather statistical data. It involves use of data collection tools likes online surveys, 
questionnaires, and polls. There are several ways to distribute questionnaires or 
surveys. Surveyors can reach a larger number of respondents or smaller focus groups 
with the use of online surveys for a variety of research purposes.

1.2.3 Research Proposal and Aspects
A research proposal is designed to persuade others that we have an important 
research project and that we are capable of finishing it given our work schedule and 
level of expertise. Essentially, a research proposal needs to in compass all the essential 
elements of the research procedure and provide adequate details for the readers to 
evaluate the suggested investigation. 
We need to answer the following questions about our study field and methodology: 
what we want to do, why we want to do it, and how we are going to do it. 
Why is good preparation needed?

This is important for grant of application in a competitive environment. Funding is

It assists the researcher to formulate the project, to plan, to perform and to monitor

Introduction 
We humans are the most intelligent creatures in the universe. Did you know that? 
Our exceptional intelligence allows us to make use of information that has been passed 
down through the generations. There are three equally important stages of human 
understanding -
●
●
namely preservation,
●
●
transmission, 
●
●
and advancement. 
Research contributes to the expansion of human understanding, which in turn 
allows for the creation and transmission of an up-to-date knowledge reservoir. 
Continuously striving to add to the enormous reservoir of knowledge in every 
conceivable sector, humans construct upon the documented and amassed information 
of the past, allowing the human race to progress. As researchers, it is our responsibility 
to check the literature to make sure that similar questions have been answered. We 
must have a thorough understanding of all prior work, theory, and research that pertains 
to the research topic. In order to guarantee such familiarity, we must do an exhaustive 
evaluation of Research and theoretical literature. 
Meaning of Review of Literature:

The longitudinal and cross-sectional studies are both observational studies. This

Characteristics of interest to us, in our study. We would not persuade non-walkers

compare multiple variables at once. For instance, with minimal extrapolation, we may 
examine the correlation between walking and cholesterol levels and demographic 
variables such as age, gender, income, and education level.

of cause-and-effect relationships. This is because such studies provide a snapshot of 
a single moment in time and do not consider what occurs before or after the snapshot. 
As a result, we can’t say for sure whether our daily walkers had low cholesterol levels 
before starting their exercise routines or if the daily walking behaviour helped to lower 
cholesterol levels that were previously high.

1.4.2: Model Building and Stages
  Model building is a crucial aspect of research methodology, especially in fields 
such as data science, engineering, and social sciences. It involves creating abstract 
representations of real-world systems or phenomena to understand, analyze, and 
predict their behavior. The process of model building in research follows several 
essential stages to develop a reliable and valid model.
Firstly, the problem must be defined clearly by identifying the objectives and 
understanding the scope, objectives, and constraints of the study. This includes 
gathering relevant data and information to understand the context and requirements of 
the model.
Next, conceptualization involves developing a theoretical framework based 
on existing literature and theories related to the problem. This helps in formulating 
hypotheses and identifying key variables. A preliminary model is then created to outline 
the relationships between different variables and components, often represented 
diagrammatically.
The data collection stage involves identifying and gathering data from primary 
and secondary sources such as surveys, experiments, observations, and databases. 
Ensuring data quality is crucial, as the data must be accurate, reliable, and relevant to 
the research problem, often requiring data cleaning and preprocessing.
In the model specification stage, the conceptual model is translated into a 
mathematical or statistical form. This involves selecting appropriate modeling 
techniques and specifying equations or algorithms. Any assumptions made during this 
stage must be clearly stated, as they can impact the model’s validity.
Model estimation involves using statistical or computational methods to estimate 
the parameters of the model, employing techniques such as regression analysis or 
machine learning algorithms. The model parameters are then calibrated to improve 
accuracy and fit to the observed data.
Validation of the model is crucial to ensure it is correctly implemented and free from 
logical or computational errors. The model’s predictions are compared with real-world 
data to assess accuracy and reliability, which may involve cross-validation, sensitivity 
analysis, and robustness checks.
Once validated, the model is implemented to analyze the research problem, make 
predictions, or provide insights. This stage involves using the model for decision-making 
or further research. Optimization of the model is also necessary based on feedback and 
results, potentially iterating through previous stages to enhance performance.
Finally, the results are interpreted in the context of the research problem, 
understanding the implications and limitations. The entire modeling process, including 
the methodology, assumptions, data sources, and findings, is documented to ensure 
transparency and reproducibility. The results are then reported clearly and concisely 
through research papers, reports, or presentations, including visualizations and 
explanations of the model’s implications.

Introduction
Sampling is a fundamental concept in research methodology that involves 
selecting a subset of individuals, items, or data points from a larger population to make 
inferences about that population. This process allows researchers to draw conclusions 
without having to study the entire population, which is often impractical or impossible.
Purpose of Sampling
The main purpose of sampling is to gather data in a way that is manageable and 
cost-effective while still allowing for accurate and reliable conclusions. By studying a 
representative sample, researchers can make generalizations about the broader 
population.

1. 	 Simple random sampling
	
Simple random sampling ensures that each element in the population has an 
equitable probability of being chosen as a component of the sample. It is like 
randomly selecting a name from a hat. Anonymizing the population by assigning a 
unique number to each object or person and then randomly selecting numbers is a 
method for conducting simple random sampling.
 
Conducting simple random sampling is a straightforward and cost-effective method 
that completely eliminates any potential bias in the sample process. Nevertheless, 
it lacks researcher control and may result in the selection of unrepresentative 
categories by chance.
2.	
Systematic sampling
	
Systematic sampling, often referred to as systematic clustering, involves randomly 
selecting only the first item, while the subsequent items are picked in a predetermined 
pattern. Subsequently, a rule is implemented to choose every nth item or person 
thereafter.
	
Despite the presence of randomness, the researcher has the ability to set the interval 
at which items are chosen, ensuring that the selections are not unintentionally 
grouped together.
3.  Stratified sampling
 
Stratified sampling is a method that entails the random selection of individuals from 
pre-established groups. Researchers find it advantageous to possess knowledge 
about the target population, enabling them to strategically divide it (stratify) in a 
manner that is logical and relevant to the research.
 
For instance, when studying travel patterns within a population, it would be beneficial 
to distinguish between those who possess or have access to a car and those who 
rely on public transportation.

Individuals or components within a sample are chosen based on their accessibility. If

students or co-workers who are present on campus and have spare time, and are

This type of sample can be valuable, particularly when used as an initial or preliminary

encompass a specific count of males and females, or individuals belonging to 
particular age ranges or ethnicities.

lead to a sample that is skewed towards those having enough free time and a specific 
interest in participating. It is possible that bias is inherent in the process of selecting 
categories for quotas by researchers.

3.2.7: Don’t Know” Responses
The intention behind incorporating “don’t know” options in surveys is to provide 
respondents with an opportunity to abstain from questions they’re uncertain about. 
However, this approach may backfire as respondents might opt for these choices 
to avoid engaging with the question or topic entirely. Consequently, the reliability of 
survey responses could be compromised. To mitigate this issue, it’s crucial to explore 
alternative strategies, such as removing the option entirely or introducing follow-up 
questions to glean more insightful data.
Benefits of Offering an “Other” Option
Providing an “other” response alternative empowers respondents to furnish 
additional information or elucidate their perspectives. This can be especially beneficial 
in soliciting feedback on products or services, as it permits respondents to articulate 
negative opinions or express concerns. For instance, individuals may refrain from 
endorsing a product due to perceived deficiencies in quality or usability. Allowing them 
to elaborate on their rationale enables organisations to glean valuable insights into 
consumer perceptions and refine their offerings accordingly.
Appropriate Use of “Don’t Know” Responses
While “don’t know” responses may be suitable in surveys tackling sensitive topics, 
their deployment necessitates discretion. In surveys centred on brands or products, it’s 
imperative to ensure respondents possess adequate familiarity with the subject matter 
before soliciting their opinions. Failure to do so may compel respondents to furnish 
ratings for items they have no experience with, potentially distorting the data.
Balancing Response Options for Optimal Survey Design:While “don’t know” 
responses can fulfil a purpose in specific survey configurations, it’s imperative to 
evaluate their impact on data quality and respondent engagement. Incorporating 
alternative response avenues, such as the “other” option, holds the potential to yield 
valuable insights and elevate the effectiveness of surveys.

3.2.8: Missing Data
In the realm of data analysis, the presence of missing data poses significant 
challenges, impacting the accuracy and reliability of research findings. Let’s explore the 
various types of missing data and their implications, along with strategies to address 
them effectively.
Categories of Missing Data
● 
Missing Completely at Random (MCAR): In MCAR scenarios, missing data occur 
randomly across variables, unrelated to any other factors. For example, incomplete 
survey responses due to random dropouts exemplify MCAR data.
● 
Missing at Random (MAR): Despite its name, MAR data display a systematic pattern, 
albeit explainable by observed variables. For instance, in a holiday spending survey, 
missing values may be more common among certain age groups due to privacy 
concerns rather than spending amounts themselves.
● 
Missing Not at Random (MNAR): MNAR data arise due to reasons inherent to the 
values themselves. For instance, individuals with lower incomes may intentionally 
omit reporting holiday spending amounts, thereby skewing the dataset.
Implications of Missing Data
● 
The presence of missing data introduces biases that can compromise the 
representativeness and generalizability of study findings. While MCAR and MAR 
data may be considered ignorable, MNAR data introduce non-ignorable biases that 
can potentially distort conclusions.
Strategies to Handle Missing Data
● 
Preventive Measures: Minimise missing data by designing user-friendly data 
collection forms, employing data validation techniques, and providing incentives 
to participants. Additionally, limiting the number of follow-ups and the volume of 
collected data can help mitigate risks associated with missing data.
● 
Secure Storage: Store collected data securely with multiple backups to mitigate the 
risk of data loss and ensure data integrity.
By comprehensively understanding the nuances of missing data and implementing 
proactive strategies, researchers can effectively address missing data challenges, 
thereby enhancing the reliability and robustness of their analyses
